summary: Psalm 70 is a brief urgent plea for God to act quickly. The speaker asks for deliverance from people seeking his ruin, asks that those who seek God rejoice, and ends by naming his own poverty and need while asking Yahweh not to delay.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how compressed a psalm of distress can be: danger, shame, worship, need, and trust are all held in five verses. In Book II of Psalms, it adds another David-associated prayer where need is brought directly before God rather than hidden or softened.

context.author: The heading says, “By David,” but Psalms headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection; readers differ on how much historical information this heading gives.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later adopted by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Psalm 70 cannot be securely assigned to a single date. It belongs to a Psalter whose poems and collections developed over centuries, from the monarchy through the postexilic period.
context.setting: An unnamed crisis in which the speaker is threatened by enemies and asks God for quick help.
context.literaryForm: A short Hebrew prayer poem or lament, with a heading and tightly paired lines of request, reversal, praise, and personal need.

outline.heading: Heading and urgent plea
outline.note: The psalm is introduced for the Chief Musician, associated with David, and framed as a reminder; the first request is for God to hurry and help.

outline.heading: Enemies asked to be shamed
outline.note: The speaker asks that those seeking his life and enjoying his trouble be disappointed, confounded, turned back, and ashamed.

outline.heading: God-seekers called to joy
outline.note: The prayer widens from the speaker’s danger to all who seek God and love God’s salvation, asking that they rejoice and exalt God.

outline.heading: Need and final appeal
outline.note: The speaker names himself poor and needy, calls God his help and deliverer, and repeats the plea for quick action.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. By David. A reminder. Hurry, God, to deliver me. Come quickly to help me, Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives both the heading and the chapter’s main pressure: the speaker is asking God for immediate rescue.

keyVerses.text: Let all those who seek you rejoice and be glad in you. Let those who love your salvation continually say, “Let God be exalted!”
keyVerses.why: This verse turns from enemies and danger to the wider community of people who seek God and celebrate his salvation.

keyVerses.text: But I am poor and needy. Come to me quickly, God. You are my help and my deliverer. Yahweh, don’t delay.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the psalm’s personal need, trust, and urgency into one closing appeal.

themes: the voice of the poor and needy
joy among those who seek God

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with “For the Chief Musician. By David. A reminder.”?
questions.answer: The heading places the psalm within the worshiping and transmitted Psalter. “By David” may be read as authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers differ on how much biographical information it supplies. “A reminder” is part of the heading here, but the chapter itself does not explain the exact performance setting.

questions.question: What kind of situation is the speaker in?
questions.answer: The speaker asks God to deliver him and says that others “seek my soul” and “desire my ruin.” The chapter does not identify the enemies, the place, or the event. It gives the experience of danger more than a historical report of the crisis.

questions.question: What does “my soul” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, “my soul” is the life or self that enemies seek. A first-time reader should not reduce it to an abstract inner part only; the line is about the speaker being threatened. The parallel line, “those who desire my ruin,” helps clarify the danger.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask for enemies to be disappointed, confounded, and disgraced?
questions.answer: Verses 2-3 ask God to reverse the enemies’ hostile aims and public mockery. This is an imprecatory kind of prayer, meaning it asks God to act against wrongdoers. The chapter voices distress and appeal to God; it does not give readers permission to carry out revenge themselves.

questions.question: What does “Aha! Aha!” show?
questions.answer: The repeated cry presents the enemies as mocking or gloating over the speaker’s trouble. The psalm asks that this shameful speech be turned back on them. Although the precise scene is unnamed, the doubled cry makes their gloating audible.

questions.question: Why does verse 4 suddenly mention people who seek God?
questions.answer: The prayer is not only about the speaker’s rescue. It also asks that all who seek God rejoice, be glad, and keep saying, “Let God be exalted!” The contrast is sharp: some seek the speaker’s ruin, while others seek God and love his salvation.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by “salvation”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “salvation” is connected to God’s help and deliverance. Verse 1 asks God to deliver; verse 5 calls God “my help and my deliverer.” The word is broader than a private feeling, but the psalm does not spell out every dimension of it.

questions.question: Why does the speaker call himself “poor and needy”?
questions.answer: The phrase names vulnerability and dependence in the middle of danger. It does not give a financial biography by itself, though it may include material weakness. In the poem, it explains why the speaker pleads, “Come to me quickly, God.”

questions.question: Does the repeated request for speed show impatience with God?
questions.answer: The chapter repeatedly asks for quick help: “Hurry,” “Come quickly,” and “don’t delay.” It does not pause to explain whether the speaker feels impatience, fear, faith, or all of these together. What it clearly depicts is urgent dependence on God during trouble.

glossary.def: A musical or worship leader named in the heading. The title points to performance, though its exact ancient role is uncertain.
A word in the heading of this psalm. The chapter does not explain whether it names a type of prayer, a liturgical use, or another function.
The title the speaker uses for God in verse 5, matching the request for deliverance in verse 1.
The speaker’s description of himself in verse 5, expressing vulnerability and need for God’s quick help.
